flashcard_questions.a: The process by which the world becomes more interconnected through increased trade and cultural exchange.
A business that has operations in more than one country.
A tax placed on imported goods to raise their price and reduce demand.
A group of countries that agree to trade more freely under common rules.
When the value of a country's imports exceeds the value of its exports.

flashcard_questions.q: When does a country have a trade surplus?
flashcard_questions.a: When exports are worth more than imports.
The price of one currency expressed in terms of another.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to imported materials when the pound weakens?
flashcard_questions.a: They cost more, pushing up costs for businesses that rely on imports.

flashcard_questions.q: What happens to UK exports when the pound strengthens?
flashcard_questions.a: They become more expensive abroad, so demand may fall.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the main risk of imposing tariffs on imports?
flashcard_questions.a: Other countries may retaliate with tariffs on UK exports.

flashcard_questions.q: Which trade agreement replaced NAFTA in 2020?
What is the number of countries in the European Union?
Why did James Dyson move his headquarters to Singapore?
flashcard_questions.a: It is closer to growing Asian markets such as China.

flashcard_questions.q: What sum did Tesla invest in its Shanghai factory?
What harm can cheaper imports do to UK producers?
flashcard_questions.a: They may struggle to compete, which can cause job losses.

notes: 15 cards: 7 term→definition (globalisation, MNC, tariff, trade bloc, trade deficit, trade surplus, exchange rate), 2 exchange-rate effect cards, 4 concept→named example (USMCA, EU 27, Dyson Singapore, Tesla $5bn Shanghai), 2 single-fact disadvantage cards (tariff retaliation, import competition). Dropped the Coca-Cola 200-countries and Primark stats to stay at 15 — the named cases already cover MNC behaviour.
